findings.issue: The rationale supplied 'accounts' as the object handed down; Luke's printed unit says 'them' in a prologue about events/accounts and does not specify a completed written account as the transmission mode.
findings.after: Both describe reception from earlier witnesses. Hebrews says salvation was first spoken through the Lord and confirmed by those who heard; Luke says those who were eyewitnesses and servants of the word from the beginning handed them down to us. The hearing/eyewitness and confirmed/handed-down forms do not identify the groups or authors as one or specify one identical transmission process.

findings.issue: The possessive 'Holy Spirit's distributions' could prematurely settle the genitive or imply the Spirit is the grammatical acting subject in Hebrews, whose main subject is God. The actual of-the-Holy-Spirit construction and the distinct Corinthian Spirit-subject should remain explicit.
findings.after: Both connect mighty deeds or acts of power with distributions associated with the Spirit and will. Hebrews names God bearing witness through signs, mighty deeds and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to His own will; Corinthians names the one Spirit working and distributing to each as He wills. Their witness and communal-gift purposes and different grammatical acting roles remain explicit.
